items.set_title: RC1: Philosophy of Time and Memory
items.passage: We say that time passes, as if it were a river carrying us along, but the metaphor hides how many different times we actually live in. There is clock time, measured in seconds and deadlines, and there is lived time, measured in waiting, in boredom, in sudden joy. A year of grief can feel longer than a decade of routine. An afternoon with a friend can pass in what seems like minutes, while an afternoon in a queue can stretch into hours. The difference is not in the clocks, which tick at the same rate, but in attention and memory. Time feels long when it is filled with new experiences that memory must record, and short when it is filled with repetition that memory discards. This is why childhood summers seem endless and adult years seem to accelerate: childhood is dense with firsts, adulthood with routine. Philosophers have argued for centuries about whether time is real or an invention of the mind, but the practical question is different. It is how we should spend the time we have, given that its felt length depends on how we live it. A life filled with novelty, attention and reflection will feel longer in retrospect, even if it lasts the same number of years. A life of unexamined routine will feel short, not because it was, but because so little of it was noticed. The implication is unsettling. We cannot add years to a life, but we can add life to years, by breaking routine, by paying attention, and by remembering deliberately. Time, in this account, is not only something that happens to us. It is something we make, in the small choices of what to notice, what to repeat, and what to allow ourselves to forget. Calendars and deadlines impose clock time on lived time, and much of modern anxiety comes from the collision between the two. A project that takes a week on paper may take a month in lived experience, because it involves waiting, uncertainty and the slow work of thinking, none of which appears on a schedule. Managers who treat the schedule as reality may conclude that workers are lazy, when in fact they are living in a different kind of time. A more humane approach would allow for both kinds of time, setting deadlines that respect the rhythm of the work, and recognising that some tasks, like writing or designing, cannot be hurried without being damaged. That recognition does not make deadlines disappear, but it makes them honest, and honesty about time is the beginning of honesty about work.

items.passage: Trust is the most economical institution a society possesses, and also the most fragile. When trust is present, people can cooperate without constant monitoring, contracts can be short, and promises can be taken at face value. When it is absent, every transaction needs a lawyer, every promise needs a guarantee, and the cost of doing anything rises sharply. Trust is not the same as faith. It is a bet on future behaviour, made without full information, based on past reliability. It is built slowly, through repeated small acts of keeping one's word, and it is destroyed quickly, often by a single betrayal that rewrites the whole history in retrospect. Institutions face the same logic. A bank, a court or a newspaper does not earn trust by declaring itself trustworthy, but by behaving predictably over time, by admitting mistakes promptly, and by accepting scrutiny when it would rather not. The paradox is that trust, once lost, cannot be bought back by the same behaviour that built it. A bank that has failed its customers must do more than resume normal service; it must accept constraints it would not have accepted before, because the bet has changed. The depositor is no longer betting that the bank will behave well; she is betting that it cannot behave badly. Understanding this matters because trust is often treated as a mood, something that rises and falls with sentiment. In fact it is a structure, built of repeated actions and the expectations they create, and like any structure it can be maintained, neglected or deliberately demolished, but it cannot be wished back into existence. Banks after a crisis illustrate the point sharply, because they must persuade depositors to return, and depositors remember the failure longer than the recovery. A bank that resumes lending, publishes reassuring statements and sponsors community events may still find that trust returns slowly, because trust is not restored by the absence of failure but by the presence of constraint. Depositors want to see independent audits, limits on risk taking, and managers who accept lower pay when the bank performs poorly. Those constraints are costly and unwelcome, yet they are the price of rebuilding a structure that was demolished, and a bank that refuses to pay it may find that its customers have moved on, not in anger but in quiet, permanent caution.

items.set_title: RC3: The Political Economy of Debt
items.passage: Debt is often discussed as if it were a technical matter, a question of interest rates and repayment schedules. In fact it is a moral question disguised as a technical one. To borrow is to transfer resources from the future to the present, to enjoy now what a later generation must pay for. That transfer can be justified, when the borrowing creates something the future can use: a railway, a school, a hospital, a skill. It is harder to justify when the borrowing pays for consumption that leaves nothing behind, a feast today and a bill tomorrow. The difficulty is that the future cannot negotiate. It has no vote, no voice and no representative at the table where the borrowing is decided. The present generation therefore acts as both borrower and judge, and it is unsurprising that it often judges in its own favour. This is why rules about debt matter. A household that borrows to educate a child is making a different choice from a household that borrows to fund a holiday, even if the interest rate is the same. A government that borrows to build infrastructure is making a different choice from one that borrows to pay today's salaries. The numbers look similar; the moral content does not. None of this means debt should be avoided. A society that never borrows may also be a society that never builds. It means debt should be judged not by its size alone but by what it leaves behind, and by whether the generation that must repay it would have agreed to the bargain if it had been asked. Student loans are a clear example, because a young person borrows against a future income that does not yet exist, to pay for an education whose value is uncertain. If the education leads to a good job, the debt may be justified, and the future self may thank the present self for the gamble. If it does not, the debt becomes a burden that shapes every later choice, delaying marriage, home ownership and further study. The borrower, at eighteen, cannot know which outcome will occur, and the lender, who profits either way, has little incentive to warn her. A fair system would share the risk, so that the institution that benefits from the borrowing also bears some of the cost when the gamble fails, rather than leaving the entire burden on the person least able to bear it.

Borrowing transfers resources from the future to the present, and the future cannot negotiate, vote or be represented at the table.

items.passage: Science is often presented as a body of certain facts, and scientists are often punished, in public debate, for admitting that they do not know. That punishment misunderstands how science works. A scientist who says a result is likely, within a range, is not being evasive; she is being precise. Uncertainty, stated honestly, is a measure of what is known, not a confession of ignorance. The public difficulty is that uncertainty feels like weakness. A politician who says we do not yet know is accused of dithering, while a politician who claims certainty is praised for leadership, even when the certainty is false. The result is a perverse incentive: those who know most about a subject are the most careful in their claims, while those who know least are the most confident. Expertise, in this account, is not the ability to give a single number without hesitation. It is the ability to say what is known, what is not known, and what would change the answer. A good expert is therefore recognisable not by confidence but by the quality of her doubts. She can name the evidence that would prove her wrong, and she updates her view when that evidence arrives. The test of expertise is not whether a person is ever wrong, since all experts are sometimes wrong, but whether they are wrong in a way that can be corrected, and whether they welcome the correction when it comes. Climate models illustrate the same point in a different register, because they produce ranges, not single numbers, and those ranges are often reported as if they were a failure of knowledge. A model that predicts warming of between one and a half and three degrees is not saying that scientists do not know what will happen; it is saying that the outcome depends on choices that have not yet been made, about emissions, about policy and about technology. That is a precise statement, and it is more honest than a single number that pretends the future is already decided. The public, however, often hears the range as uncertainty, and uncertainty as an excuse for inaction, when in fact the range is a call to action, because the lower end is available only if choices change, and the upper end is the price of doing nothing.

items.passage: Every language has words that refuse to travel. They carry a history, a joke, a grief or a season that has no equivalent in another tongue, and when they are translated, something is lost that no footnote can fully restore. A word for the smell of rain on dry earth, for the light of a particular afternoon, for a form of respect owed to an elder, may be rendered accurately and still feel empty, because the life around the word has not travelled with it. This does not mean translation is impossible. It means translation is a choice, not a mechanical transfer. The translator must decide what to preserve and what to let go: the literal meaning, the rhythm, the association, the joke. Each choice saves one thing and sacrifices another, and a good translation is honest about the sacrifice it has made. Cultures, like languages, lose something in every act of translation, and gain something too. A story that travels acquires new readers, new meanings and new lives, even as it leaves behind the particular soil in which it grew. The loss is real, and it should be mourned, but the gain is real as well, and it should be celebrated. To refuse translation for fear of loss would be to keep every culture locked in its own room, and to translate carelessly, pretending nothing is lost, would be to lie about what has happened. The honest position is in between: to translate with care, to name what has been lost, and to allow the translated work to live a second life that is different from, but not lesser than, the first. Film subtitles show the same trade off in miniature, because a translator must decide whether to preserve the literal words, the joke, the rhythm or the cultural reference, and cannot preserve them all. A joke that depends on a pun may be replaced by a different joke, a reference to a local celebrity may be replaced by a reference the audience will recognise, and a formal speech may be rendered in slang to preserve its tone. Viewers who compare the subtitle with the original may complain that something has been lost, and they are right, but they may miss what has been gained, which is a film that can be understood and enjoyed by people who do not speak the language. Translation, in this sense, is not a failure to be perfect, but a success in being useful, and usefulness requires choice.

items.passage: My father drew maps of a river that moved, / of a border that shifted in the night, / of a house that stood where the road now bends, / and of a village that was no longer there. // He drew them in pencil, so they could be changed, / and taught me to read the dotted lines, / the places where the map admitted it did not know, / the small, honest gaps where the land had moved on. // But at home I learned that a map is a promise, / and broken by the land itself, in its own time. // Now I draw maps of my own, / and I leave the dotted lines in, on purpose, / because a place, like a person, is never finished, / and the honest map is the one that says, / here, I do not know, and here, I am still learning.
items.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a reading of the image of the father drawing maps in pencil, so they could be changed with the later line that confirms it?
options: The father was a poor draughtsman who could not afford ink for his maps; "He drew them in pencil, so they could be changed"
The dotted lines on the map are mistakes the father forgot to erase; "the places where the map admitted it did not know"
Maps are provisional records that must admit what they do not know, because the land itself moves and outlasts any fixed line; "of a border that shifted in the night"
The father drew in pencil because he expected the river to stay exactly where it was; "and the honest map is the one that says, here, I do not know, and here, I am still learning"

Maps are provisional records that must admit what they do not know, because the land itself moves and outlasts any fixed line; "and the honest map is the one that says, here, I do not know, and here, I am still learning"
items.explanation: Pencil is chosen because it can be changed, and the dotted lines mark where the map admits it does not know. The reading has two halves, provisionality and honesty, and only the final lines confirm both: the honest map says where it does not know and where it is still learning. The line about the shifting border shows the land moves but says nothing about the map admitting what it does not know, so it confirms only half the reading. The line about the places where the map admitted it did not know contradicts the claim that the dotted lines are mistakes.

items.passage: My father drew maps of a river that moved, / of a border that shifted in the night, / of a house that stood where the road now bends, / and of a village that was no longer there. // He drew them in pencil, so they could be changed, / and taught me to read the dotted lines, / the places where the map admitted it did not know, / the small, honest gaps where the land had moved on. // But at home I learned that a map is a promise, / and broken by the land itself, in its own time. // Now I draw maps of my own, / and I leave the dotted lines in, on purpose, / because a place, like a person, is never finished, / and the honest map is the one that says, / here, I do not know, and here, I am still learning.
items.question: The poem says the father drew maps 'in pencil, so they could be changed'. Which reading best captures what the pencil means for the daughter's own maps?
options: The daughter draws in pencil too, because she believes a map should admit what it does not know and stay open to change.
The daughter draws in pencil because she copies her father's maps without improving them.
The pencil means the father's maps were unfinished, and the daughter finishes them in ink.
The pencil shows the father was careless, and the daughter corrects his mistakes.
The daughter uses pencil only for the borders that shifted in the night.
items.explanation: The father taught her to read the dotted lines, the places where the map admitted it did not know, and she now leaves the dotted lines in on purpose, because a place, like a person, is never finished. The pencil stands for that same provisional honesty in her own maps, not for copying, carelessness or a single kind of border.

items.question: A town finds that streets with more street lights have fewer accidents at night. A councillor concludes that installing more lights will reduce accidents. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
options: Residents like well-lit streets and say they feel safer walking on them at night
A few well-lit streets still have accidents, while some dim lanes have none
The well-lit streets are the main roads, which are wider, straighter and better maintained than the dimly lit lanes, and those features, not the lights, explain the safety difference
Installing lights is cheaper than widening roads or resurfacing them
Accidents also fall on streets where new speed signs were put up last year
items.explanation: If the well-lit streets are safer because they are wider and better maintained, the lights may not be the cause, so installing more lights need not reduce accidents. Feeling safer, a few exceptions and cost do not test the causal claim.

items.question: A shop raises its prices and launches a new advertisement, and sales rise by 20 percent. The owner argues the advertisement caused the rise. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the owner's argument?
options: Some customers said they liked the advertisement, while others said they had not seen it
In the same period the price of the shop's closest substitute rose sharply, driving customers to the shop regardless of its advertising
Sales also rose in a city where the advertisement was not shown, but the substitute's price rose there too and by the same amount
The advertisement cost less than the extra revenue the sales rise brought in
A rival shop that advertised heavily saw its sales fall after a product recall
items.explanation: A sharp rise in a substitute's price is an alternative cause that fully accounts for the sales rise. The city without the advertisement also had the substitute's price rise, so its sales rise is consistent with that explanation rather than a second weaken.

items.question: A firm finds that employees who work from home take fewer sick days than employees who work in the office. The firm also finds that home workers are younger on average and hold jobs that can be done remotely. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Working from home may or may not reduce sick days, because the home workers differ from office workers in age and in the kind of job they do
Working from home definitely reduces sick days, because home workers take fewer of them
Working from home increases sick days, because younger workers take fewer sick days anyway
Office work always causes more sickness than home work, whatever the job
Age has no effect on sick days, so working from home must be the cause
items.explanation: Age and job type are confounders: younger workers and remote-capable jobs may take fewer sick days for reasons unrelated to location. The data cannot separate the effect of working from home, so only the weaker conclusion is supported.

items.question: Choose the sentence in which BOTH words in capitals are used correctly.
options: The historian was METICULOUS, checking every date in the archive before she wrote a single paragraph, and CURSORY in her summary, because she examined every detail at length.
The historian was METICULOUS, because she wrote the whole book in a single afternoon without checking anything, and CURSORY in her summary, because she skimmed it in an hour.
The METICULOUS storm destroyed the town in an hour, and the CURSORY archive held every document the town had ever produced, catalogued in full.
His METICULOUS speech lasted only ten seconds and said nothing at all, and his CURSORY answer was checked three times before it was given.
The historian was METICULOUS, checking every date in the archive before she wrote a single paragraph, and CURSORY in her summary, because she skimmed it in an hour and missed the details.
items.explanation: METICULOUS means very careful and precise, and CURSORY means hasty and superficial. Only the last option uses both correctly: checking every date is meticulous, and skimming a summary in an hour is cursory. The first option misuses CURSORY, the second misuses METICULOUS, and the third and fourth misuse both, since a storm cannot be meticulous and an answer checked three times is not cursory.

items.question: Consider the following six sentences. (1) A number of workers were absent on Monday morning. (2) The committee has decided to postpone the meeting until next week. (3) Neither the teacher nor the students were present at the assembly. (4) Every one of the participants have received a certificate. (5) The quality of the products have improved this year. (6) Either the director or the managers is responsible for the decision. Which of the following combinations consists entirely of correct sentences?
options: Sentences 1, 2 and 4
Sentences 1, 2 and 5
Sentences 1, 2 and 6
Sentences 1, 2 and 3
Sentences 4, 5 and 6
items.explanation: Sentences 1, 2 and 3 are correct: a number of takes a plural verb, the committee as a single body takes a singular verb, and neither-nor with a plural nearer subject takes a plural verb. Sentence 4 needs has, sentence 5 needs has, and sentence 6 needs are.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The vaccine was ready in eleven months, a speed that surprised even its makers. (B) That speed was possible only because twenty years of earlier research had already answered the hard questions. (C) This history is often forgotten when the vaccine is described as a miracle produced overnight. (D) Forgetting it matters, because it leads the public to expect the same speed from every new treatment. (E) The lesson, then, is that rapid success is usually the visible end of a long invisible preparation. Which of the following is the correct order?
options: C-A-B-D-E
D-B-C-A-E
A-B-C-D-E
A-B-E-C-D
E-A-B-C-D
items.explanation: A states the speed, B explains it with the earlier research, C's this history needs B before it, D gives the consequence of forgetting it, and E draws the lesson. Putting C before B breaks the reference to the history.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) A forest that looks untouched may in fact have been shaped by people for centuries. (B) The trees that grow there were planted, thinned and protected by generations who lived in it. (C) These practices, invisible to a visitor, are what make the forest what it is. (D) To fence the forest off as wilderness, therefore, is to misunderstand it, and to exclude the very people who made it. (E) Conservation that ignores that history protects a landscape while losing the knowledge that sustains it. Which of the following is the correct order?
options: C-A-B-D-E
A-B-C-D-E
D-B-C-A-E
A-B-E-C-D
E-A-B-C-D
items.explanation: A states the claim, B gives the evidence of planting and thinning, C's these practices needs B before it, D draws the consequence for fencing it off, and E states the wider lesson. C before B would leave these practices without an antecedent.

items.question: The editorial on the new overnight train was ______ in its praise of the sleeper berths, which it called the best on the network; ______ in its judgement of the timetable, which left the largest city unserved at night; and ______ in its conclusion, calling the service a success for leisure travellers and a failure for business travellers.
options: unstinting; blunt; split
unstinting; mild; split
guarded; blunt; split
unstinting; blunt; unanimous
guarded; mild; unanimous
items.explanation: The three blanks interact, and the third can only be fixed from the first two together. Praise that calls the berths the best on the network is unstinting, not guarded, and a timetable that leaves the largest city unserved makes the judgement blunt, not mild. A conclusion that calls the service a success for one group and a failure for another is split, not unanimous. The sentence gives no explicit contrast word, so the split conclusion has to be inferred from the praise and the criticism. Each distractor fails exactly one blank, except the last, which fails all three.

items.question: The cartoon shows a teacher holding a key labelled Curiosity in front of a locked door labelled Learning, while a crowd behind her pushes a battering ram labelled Exams toward the same door. Which of the following best captures the meaning of the cartoon?
options: Teachers should carry keys at all times, and schools should buy more locks
Examinations are the fastest way to learn, and the cartoon recommends more of them
The battering ram is a useful tool, and the crowd is helping the teacher open the door
Learning is a locked room that nobody can ever enter, whatever method is used
Curiosity opens learning gently, while forcing entry through examinations breaks the door it was meant to open
items.explanation: The key and the battering ram are two ways of entering the same door: curiosity opens it, while examinations force it. The cartoon contrasts the gentle method with the violent one; it does not recommend the ram or claim the room can never be entered.

If print readers are older and shrinking while digital readers are younger and growing, the future audience is digital, which supports investing in the digital edition despite the current print profit. Print advertising being stable would argue against change. A rival closing is a temporary gain. A new press would lock money into print. A government grant for print would support keeping print.
options: Print advertising revenue has been stable for the last three years
A rival newspaper closed last year, leaving its readers to choose a new paper
Print readers are mostly over 60 and shrinking by 8 percent a year, while digital readers are mostly under 40 and growing by 15 percent a year
The paper has just bought a new printing press with a ten-year life
The state government offers a grant for newspapers that keep a print edition
items.passage: A 90-year-old regional newspaper has seen its print circulation fall from 4 lakh copies a day to 2.4 lakh in five years, while its free website reaches 30 lakh readers a month but earns only a tenth of the revenue per reader that print earns. The print edition still makes a profit because of loyal older readers and local advertising, but the printing press is 30 years old and needs a 6 crore rupee replacement. The editor wants to close the print edition within two years and move fully digital, arguing that the future audience is online and that the press replacement money should fund digital journalism instead. The circulation head warns that closing print would lose the most loyal readers, who pay the highest price, and that digital advertising rates are falling as social media takes the market. The advertising head notes that local businesses still prefer print ads because they trust the paper, while national advertisers have already moved online. The owner must decide before the press replacement contract is signed, because the contract commits the firm for ten years. A survey shows that 70 percent of print readers are over 55, while 80 percent of website readers are under 40, and that website readers spend an average of four minutes a day on the site compared with 40 minutes for print readers. The website earns money from display advertising, but rates have fallen by a third in two years as advertisers move to social media. The paper's loyal print readers include many local businesses that have advertised for decades and who say they trust the paper more than any other local medium. The digital team has 25 journalists and wants funding for video reporting and data journalism that the print edition cannot support.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support moving fully digital within two years?
items.set_title: DM1: The Newspaper at a Crossroads
DM1: The Newspaper at a Crossroads
items.question: A year later, the owner has kept print and funded digital from the press replacement money in part. Print circulation is 2.4 lakh copies a day and each print reader spends 40 minutes a day on the paper, while the website reaches 30 lakh readers a month who spend 4 minutes a day. The advertising head reports that a print reader is worth ten times a website reader in revenue. Counting the website's monthly readers as daily readers for this comparison, is the print audience's total daily reading time larger than the website's, and by what factor?
options: Print is larger, at about 1.25 times the website total
Print is larger, at about 10 times the website total
Print is larger, at about 4 times the website total
Print is smaller, at about 0.8 times the website total
Print is smaller, at about 0.08 times the website total
items.explanation: Print gives 2.4 lakh readers times 40 minutes, which is 96 lakh reader-minutes a day. The website gives 30 lakh readers times 4 minutes, which is 120 lakh reader-minutes a day. Print divided by the website is 96 divided by 120, which is 0.8, so print is smaller, not larger. The 1.25 option is the ratio the wrong way round, the 10 option is the revenue-per-reader ratio rather than reading time, and 0.08 is a decimal-place error.

items.set_title: DM1: The Newspaper at a Crossroads
items.question: The owner has decided to keep print and grow digital slowly. The editor now asks for a rule that will stop the paper from ever again having to choose between its loyal print readers and its digital future in a single rushed decision. Which rule does BOTH things: it decides the press replacement and the digital budget separately, on their own horizons, and it never commits the firm to one future for ten years in a single contract?
options: The print edition will be closed within two years, whatever the loyal readers say, because the future audience is online
The press replacement and the digital budget will be decided separately, on their own ten-year and two-year horizons, and no single contract will commit the firm to one future for ten years
The website will be closed, because print readers spend ten times as long on the paper as website readers spend online
The firm will sign the ten-year press contract at once, so that the decision is made and cannot be revisited
The press replacement and the digital budget will be decided separately, but the firm will still sign one ten-year contract covering both, so the decision is made once
items.explanation: The rule must do two things: separate the press decision from the digital decision, and avoid a single contract that locks the firm into one future for ten years. Only the second option does both. The last option separates the decisions but still signs one ten-year contract covering both, so it fails the second condition. Closing print abandons the loyal readers, closing the website abandons the future audience, and signing the press contract at once repeats the rushed decision.

If the product was sold as low risk to people who needed safe savings, the mis-selling is clear and the case for full compensation and disclosure is strongest. The staff following a script shows a system failure, not an excuse. A rival selling the same product does not make this sale fair. Bonuses for selling explain the motive but do not justify the sale. The product being legal does not make the way it was sold honest.
options: The product was sold as low risk to retired customers who needed safe savings and could not afford to lose money
The staff who sold the product followed the script given by head office
A rival bank sells the same product to its customers
Staff received a bonus for selling this product
The product itself is legal and approved by the regulator
items.passage: A large private bank sold a complex investment product to 12,000 retail customers over two years, describing it in brochures as a safe alternative to fixed deposits. The product in fact carried a risk of losing up to 30 percent of the invested amount if a stock index fell, a risk buried in the fine print on page 14 of the agreement. Around 3,000 customers, many of them retired, have lost money and filed complaints, and the regulator has asked the bank for an explanation. The bank's retail head argues that the risk was disclosed in the agreement, that customers signed it, and that the bank should fight the complaints in court rather than pay compensation, because paying would invite claims from all 12,000 buyers. The compliance head warns that the marketing material was misleading, that the regulator can impose a large fine, and that fighting retired customers in court will damage the bank's reputation for years. The chief executive must decide this week, because the regulator has set a deadline for the bank's response and a consumer group is planning a public protest outside the bank's head office. The consumer group has collected 2,000 complaints and plans a protest outside the head office on Friday. The regulator has set a deadline of one week for the bank's response and has the power to fine the bank and to order compensation. The retail head has warned the board that paying all 12,000 buyers would cost far more than paying the 3,000 who complained, while the compliance head has warned that fighting in court could take five years and would keep the story in the news throughout.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support paying full compensation to the affected customers?

A week later, the regulator has set a deadline of one week for the bank's response, and the consumer group has collected 2,000 complaints and plans a protest outside the head office on Friday. Five facts have come to light. (A) The product was described in brochures as a safe alternative to fixed deposits, while the risk of losing up to 30 percent was buried on page 14 of the agreement. (B) Around 3,000 customers, many of them retired, have lost money and filed complaints. (C) Paying all 12,000 buyers would cost far more than paying the 3,000 who complained. (D) Fighting in court could take five years and would keep the story in the news throughout. (E) The risk was disclosed in the agreement, and customers signed it. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the chief executive compensate ALL 12,000 purchasers now, rather than fight in court?
options: (A), (C) and (E)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (E)
(C), (D) and (E)
(A), (B) and (D)
items.explanation: The decision is now explicit: compensate all 12,000 purchasers, not only the 3,000 who complained. Compensating all is justified by three legs: the marketing was misleading, whatever the fine print said (A); the harm is real, with around 3,000 customers, many of them retired, having lost money (B); and fighting would keep the story in the news for five years (D). Fact (C) now points decisively against the decision as stated: paying all 12,000 costs far more than paying only the 3,000 who complained, so any triple containing (C) argues against compensating all, which rules out the second and fourth options. Fact (E) is the retail head's argument for fighting, which rules out the first and third options. Only (A), (B) and (D) supports compensating all purchasers now.

items.question: The bank now proposes: every brochure will state the largest possible loss on the same page, and compliance will approve every brochure, but the approval need only happen once a year for the whole product range. Which of the following best assesses the proposal?
options: It is adequate on both disclosure and approval, because same-page loss disclosure plus compliance approval removes the mis-selling risk.
It is adequate on approval but not on disclosure, because stating the loss does not help customers who cannot read the brochure.
It fails on both disclosure and approval, because it discloses nothing and involves no compliance check.
It is unnecessary, because customers signed the agreement, so the bank has no further duty.
It is adequate on disclosure but not on approval, because a single annual approval cannot catch a new brochure issued mid-year.
items.explanation: Stating the largest possible loss on the same page in the same size of print is exactly the disclosure the passage calls for, so the disclosure limb is adequate. But an approval that happens only once a year for the whole range cannot review a brochure issued mid-year, so a misleading brochure could still reach customers, and the approval limb is not adequate. Option A misses that timing gap. Option B misidentifies the weak limb. Option C misdescribes the proposal. Option D repeats the retail head's argument, which the compliance head's warning defeats.

If the same material failed in two earlier buildings, the risk is known and proven, not theoretical, which makes using it again indefensible. The material being cheaper and the project being behind schedule are pressures, not justifications. The rival using it does not make it safe. A new test that has not been run cannot support the choice.
options: The cheaper material would save 2 crore rupees on the project
The project is already six months behind schedule
A rival builder uses the same material in its projects
The same material was linked to cracks in two earlier buildings built by this firm
A new test for the material has been announced but not yet run
items.passage: A construction firm is building a 20-storey residential tower with 400 flats, most of them already sold to families who have paid advances. The project manager has found that using a cheaper cement mix would save 2 crore rupees and help the firm meet its deadline, but the firm's own engineer has warned that the cheaper mix has not been tested for a building of this height and that the supplier cannot provide a full safety certificate. The firm's owner is under pressure from lenders to finish on time, and the sales team has promised buyers possession by December. The engineer wants to use the standard mix, which costs more and would delay the project by two months, and to inform buyers of the delay. The owner argues that the cheaper mix has been used in smaller buildings without problems, that the delay would cost the firm its reputation with buyers, and that the engineer is being overcautious. The structural consultant, who must sign the safety certificate, has said privately that the consultant will not sign if the cheaper mix is used. The buyers have paid advances of up to 40 lakh rupees each and many have taken home loans that they are already repaying. The lenders have said the loan will be reviewed if the project is delayed by more than two months. The structural consultant is an independent firm that has certified 30 towers in the city and has refused to sign certificates for two other builders who used cheaper materials. The firm's owner has built 12 residential projects in 20 years without a safety incident.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support using the standard mix despite the delay?

A month later, the lenders have said the loan will be reviewed if the project is delayed by more than two months, and buyers who have paid advances of up to 40 lakh rupees each are asking when they can move in. Five facts have come to light. (A) The cheaper mix has not been tested for a building of this height, and the supplier cannot provide a full safety certificate. (B) The structural consultant, who must sign the safety certificate, has said privately that the consultant will not sign if the cheaper mix is used. (C) Using the cheaper mix would save 2 crore rupees and help the firm meet its deadline. (D) The cheaper mix has been used in smaller buildings without problems. (E) The firm's own engineer has warned that the cheaper mix is untested for a 20-storey tower. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the owner use the standard mix and inform buyers of the delay?
options: (A), (C) and (D)
(B), (C) and (E)
(A), (B) and (E)
(A), (B) and (D)
(C), (D) and (E)
items.explanation: Using the standard mix is justified by three legs: the mix is untested at this height (A), the independent consultant will not certify it (B), and the firm's own engineer has warned against it (E). (C) argues for the cheaper mix, and (D) is about smaller buildings, which do not prove safety at 20 storeys. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that points the wrong way.

items.question: The firm now proposes a new policy: the standard mix will be used unless the cheaper mix has been tested for a building of that height, and buyers will be told of any delay before they pay their next instalment. Which of the following best assesses the policy?
options: It is adequate on disclosure but not on safety, because the cheaper mix may still be used without the structural consultant's certificate, which the consultant has said will not be signed if the cheaper mix is used.
It is adequate on both safety and disclosure, because testing the cheaper mix removes the risk and telling buyers removes the information gap.
It is adequate on safety but not on disclosure, because buyers who have already paid advances are not told anything.
It fails on both safety and disclosure, because it allows the cheaper mix without testing and tells buyers nothing.
It is unnecessary, because the cheaper mix has already been used safely in smaller buildings.
items.explanation: The disclosure limb is adequate, since buyers are told of any delay before they pay more, which is what the engineer asked for. The safety limb is not adequate, because the policy asks only for testing, while the passage says the structural consultant will not sign a certificate if the cheaper mix is used at all, so a tested cheaper mix could still go into the tower unsigned. Option B misses the certificate gap. Option C reverses the two limbs. Option D misdescribes the policy, which does require testing and does tell buyers. Option E repeats the owner's argument, which the passage shows the consultant's refusal defeats.

If the donor's child scored far below the cut-off, admitting the child would be a clear breach of merit and would be indefensible if discovered. The donor offering to fund a library is a temptation, not a justification. A past donation and the admissions head being new do not change the merit facts. Other universities doing the same does not make it right.
options: The donor has offered to fund a new library for the university
The donor's child scored far below the published cut-off for admission
The donor gave a large gift to the university five years ago
The admissions head is new and wants to please the trustees
Other universities also admit a few donor children each year
items.passage: A well-known private university receives an application from the child of a major donor who has pledged 10 crore rupees for a new science block. The child scored well below the published cut-off for the university's flagship engineering programme, while 200 other applicants who scored above the cut-off were rejected for lack of seats. The vice-chancellor is under pressure from the trustees to admit the donor's child, arguing that the donation will fund laboratories that benefit thousands of students and that one seat will not be noticed. The admissions head argues that the university's prospectus promises admission on merit, that the rejected applicants include students from poor families who studied for years to clear the cut-off, and that the admission would leak and destroy the university's reputation. The donor has said privately that the donation depends on the admission, and the science block is already half built with money the university borrowed. The admissions committee must decide before the term starts in three weeks. The trustees include the donor, two alumni and three academics, and the vice-chancellor needs their support for the science block loan. The 200 rejected applicants include 40 students from poor families who scored above the cut-off after years of preparation, and their parents have written to the university asking how admissions are decided. The science block is half built and the university has borrowed 6 crore rupees to pay the builders, who have said they will stop work if the next payment is late. The admissions committee meets in two days and must publish its decision before the term starts.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support refusing the donor's child?

Two days later, the 200 rejected applicants include 40 students from poor families who scored above the cut-off after years of preparation, and their parents have written asking how admissions are decided. The science block is half built and the university has borrowed 6 crore rupees to pay the builders. Five facts have come to light. (A) The prospectus promises admission on merit, and the donor's child scored well below the published cut-off. (B) The donor has said privately that the donation depends on the admission. (C) The science block is half built with borrowed money, and builders will stop work if the next payment is late. (D) The 200 rejected applicants include 40 students from poor families who scored above the cut-off. (E) The trustees include the donor, two alumni and three academics. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the admissions committee refuse the donor's child?
options: (A), (C) and (E)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (E)
(A), (B) and (D)
(C), (D) and (E)
items.explanation: Refusing is justified by three legs: the prospectus promise and the cut-off make the admission a breach of the university's own word (A), the donation is conditional, so admitting the child is a purchase, not a judgement (B), and 200 better-qualified applicants, including 40 from poor families, would be displaced (D). (C) argues for admitting, since it describes the financial pressure, and (E) is about the composition of the trustees, not a reason to refuse. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that does not support refusal.

items.question: The committee has refused the donor's child and the donor has withdrawn the pledge. The university now asks for a rule that will stop donations from ever again deciding admissions. Which rule does BOTH things: it decides admissions only against the published cut-off by the admissions committee, and it bars any donor, trustee or vice-chancellor from intervening in an individual case, with every decision published?
options: The vice-chancellor will decide admissions personally, but will keep the reasons private
Donors will be allowed to buy one seat a year, provided the amount is large enough
Admissions will be decided only against the published cut-off by the admissions committee, and no donor, trustee or vice-chancellor may intervene in an individual case, with every decision published
The published cut-off will be abolished, so that no applicant can claim to be above it
Admissions will be decided only against the published cut-off by the admissions committee, but individual decisions will be kept secret, so that donors cannot complain about them
items.explanation: The rule must do two things: decide admissions only against the published cut-off, and bar any intervention in individual cases with every decision published. Only the third option does both. The last option keeps the cut-off but hides individual decisions, so it fails the second condition. Letting the vice-chancellor decide personally repeats the problem, selling one seat a year legalises it, and abolishing the cut-off removes the only objective standard.

If the scientist's absence would halt a project worth 30 crore rupees, the firm has a concrete commercial reason to act now rather than wait for the person to leave. The scientist being the only expert is the problem itself. A rival offering a higher salary explains the risk but does not show the cost. Junior staff being unhappy is a separate issue. The scientist having no written contract is a process gap, not evidence of the cost of losing the person.
options: The scientist is the only person in the firm who understands the core process
A rival firm has offered the scientist a higher salary
Junior staff are unhappy that the scientist gets special treatment
The scientist has no written employment contract
The scientist's absence for even a month would halt a project worth 30 crore rupees in orders
items.passage: A pharmaceutical research firm depends on one senior scientist who understands a complex drug synthesis process that no one else in the firm can reproduce. The scientist refuses to document the process, declines to train juniors, and has told the head of research that the knowledge is the scientist's own job security. The firm has offered the scientist a large pay rise, a promotion and a research budget, but the scientist has refused all of them and now wants a guarantee of lifetime employment in writing. The head of research warns that if the scientist falls ill or resigns, a project worth 30 crore rupees in orders will stop, and that the firm is effectively held hostage by one person. The human resources head argues that giving a lifetime guarantee would set a dangerous precedent and would be unfair to 200 other employees. The chief executive must decide before the scientist's current contract ends in two months, and the scientist has already been approached by two rival firms. The scientist joined the firm eight years ago and built the synthesis process from an idea in a research paper, working alone for three years before the first successful batch. The project is worth 30 crore rupees in orders from two large drug makers who have said they will move to a rival if deliveries stop. The scientist has been approached twice by rival firms and has told colleagues that the offers are attractive. The head of research has asked two junior scientists to try to reproduce the process, but both have said they need the senior scientist's notes, which do not exist.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support acting now to reduce the firm's dependence on the scientist?
items.set_title: DM5: The Scientist Who Will Not Share
DM5: The Scientist Who Will Not Share
items.question: A month later, the scientist has been approached twice by rival firms and has told colleagues the offers are attractive. The head of research has asked two junior scientists to reproduce the process, but both have said they need the senior scientist's notes, which do not exist. Five facts have come to light. (A) The scientist refuses to document the process, declines to train juniors, and says the knowledge is the scientist's own job security. (B) If the scientist falls ill or resigns, a project worth 30 crore rupees in orders will stop. (C) The scientist has said a lifetime guarantee is the only offer that would be accepted, and has hinted the scientist will leave without it. (D) Giving a lifetime guarantee would set a dangerous precedent and would be unfair to 200 other employees. (E) The scientist joined the firm eight years ago and built the process alone over three years. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the chief executive refuse the lifetime guarantee while protecting the project?
options: (A), (B) and (D)
(A), (C) and (E)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (E)
(C), (D) and (E)
items.explanation: Refusing the guarantee while protecting the project is justified by three legs: the scientist is deliberately withholding the knowledge the firm needs (A), the firm is hostage to one person on a 30 crore project (B), and a lifetime guarantee would reward that behaviour and set a precedent for 200 others (D). Fact (C) now argues for giving the guarantee, since it is the only offer the scientist would accept and comes with a hinted resignation, so any triple containing (C) points the wrong way. Fact (E) is history that explains the scientist's position, not a reason to refuse the guarantee. The fourth option has two right facts and the history in place of the precedent leg, so it is the near miss.

items.question: The scientist has left and the project has been rebuilt by the juniors over a year. The firm now asks for a rule that will stop any one person from ever again holding a 30 crore project hostage. Which rule best prevents a recurrence?
options: Critical knowledge will be left with the person who created it, because only that person understands it
Lifetime guarantees will be offered to anyone who refuses to document their work, so that they stay
Junior scientists will not be allowed to ask senior scientists for their notes
The firm will depend on one scientist for each project, so that responsibility is always clear
No process on which a major project depends may rest with one person: every critical process must be documented, taught to at least two colleagues, and reviewed every year
items.explanation: The rule attacks the cause directly: undocumented knowledge held by one person. Leaving knowledge with its creator repeats the hostage position, offering lifetime guarantees for refusing to document rewards the behaviour, and depending on one scientist per project repeats the single point of failure.

items.passage: Two mid-sized accounting firms have merged, and the combined firm now has 40 partners and 300 staff doing the same work in two offices in the same city. The merger plan requires cutting 60 jobs to remove duplication, and the managing partners must choose who goes. One option is to retrench the 60 most recently hired staff, who are mostly under 30 and cheaper to employ, on a last-in-first-out basis. A second option is to retrench 60 older staff who are paid more and whose skills overlap most with the other firm's partners, which would save more money. A third option is to offer voluntary retirement to older staff with a generous package, and to retrain the rest. The merged firm also has 20 unfilled client-facing roles that retrained staff could fill. The younger staff argue that last-in-first-out punishes them for being new and for having no say in the merger. The older staff argue that they built the client base over decades and that losing them would lose clients. The union has warned that any forced retrenchment will lead to a legal challenge, and the merger agreement requires the combined firm to show a cost saving within one year. The merger agreement requires the combined firm to show a cost saving of 5 crore rupees within one year, and the managing partners have told the board the saving will come from removing duplication. The union has 200 members across the two firms and has warned that any forced retrenchment will be challenged in court, a process that could take two years. The older staff include 20 partners who have been with the firms for over 20 years, while the younger staff include 60 people hired in the last three years. The finance team has costed the voluntary retirement option: each older staff member costs the firm about Rs 30 lakh a year in salary and benefits, and the retirement package costs about Rs 12 lakh once, so each person who accepts saves about Rs 18 lakh in the first year after the package. The team expects about 40 of the 60 eligible older staff to accept, which would save about Rs 7.2 crore in the first year, comfortably above the Rs 5 crore target in the merger agreement.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support protecting the older staff rather than retrenching them, even though retrenching them would save more money, by showing BOTH that the older staff hold revenue the firm would lose AND that clients would follow them if they left?
options: The older staff are paid more than the younger staff, so retrenching them would save the most money
The older staff hold the client relationships that generate 70 percent of the merged firm's revenue, and clients have said they will follow those staff to a rival if they leave
The younger staff were hired in the last three years and are cheaper to employ
The merger agreement requires the combined firm to show a cost saving of 5 crore rupees within one year
The older staff hold the client relationships that generate 70 percent of the merged firm's revenue, but clients have said they will stay with the firm whatever happens to the staff
items.explanation: Protecting the older staff needs two things: the revenue they hold, and the fact that clients would follow them. Only the second option gives both: the older staff hold relationships generating 70 percent of revenue, and clients have said they will follow those staff to a rival. The last option gives the revenue but removes the threat, since clients would stay anyway. The pay difference argues for retrenching the older staff, the younger staff's cost argues for retrenching the younger staff, and the merger target argues for the larger saving.

items.question: A month later, the union has warned that any forced retrenchment will be challenged in court, a process that could take two years, and the merger agreement requires a cost saving of 5 crore rupees within one year. Five facts have come to light. (A) The older staff include 20 partners who have been with the firms for over 20 years and built the client base. (B) The younger staff argue that last-in-first-out punishes them for being new and for having no say in the merger. (C) Voluntary retirement with a generous package would let older staff leave by choice, and the rest could be retrained into the merged firm's 20 unfilled client-facing roles. The finance team expects about 40 of the 60 eligible older staff to accept, at a one-time package cost of about Rs 12 lakh each, saving about Rs 18 lakh per person in the first year after the package, or about Rs 7.2 crore in all, above the Rs 5 crore target. (D) Forced retrenchment of any group will be challenged in court and could take two years. (E) The merger plan requires cutting 60 jobs to remove duplication. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the managing partners choose voluntary retirement for the older staff over forced retrenchment of either group?
options: (A), (B) and (E)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (C)
(C), (D) and (E)
items.explanation: Voluntary retirement is supported by three legs, and only the triple (B), (C) and (D) contains all three. (B) supports it because choosing voluntary retirement avoids last-in-first-out altogether, so no younger staff are punished for being new, which is the unfairness the younger staff complain about. (C) supports it because the package lets older staff leave by choice, and the headcount now works as well as the money: about 40 acceptances remove 40 of the 60 duplicated posts, and the remaining 20 eligible staff move into the merged firm's 20 unfilled client-facing roles after retraining, so all 60 duplicated posts are removed with no forced retrenchment. The money works too: about 40 acceptances at a one-time cost of Rs 12 lakh each save about Rs 18 lakh per person in the first year, about Rs 7.2 crore in all, which beats the Rs 5 crore target. (D) supports it because forced retrenchment of either group would be challenged in court for two years, which would miss the one-year saving deadline in the merger agreement. (A) does NOT support the choice: the older staff built the client base over decades, so losing them risks losing clients, which is an argument for RETAINING older staff, not for encouraging them to leave. (E) only states the 60-job target and says nothing about which method to use, so it adds no support for voluntary retirement over forced retrenchment. Every other triple either contains (A), which argues against the choice, or contains (E) in place of (B), which leaves the unfairness of forced retrenchment unanswered.

items.question: The merger is complete and the voluntary retirements have been accepted. The board now asks for a rule that will stop a future merger from ever again having to choose who goes by age or by recency. Which rule best prevents a recurrence?
options: Future mergers will cut the 60 most recently hired staff without discussion, because last-in-first-out is simple

Any future merger will publish, before it is signed, which roles are duplicated, how the choice will be made, and what voluntary terms will be offered, so that no group learns its fate after the merger is agreed
Future mergers will cut the oldest staff without discussion, because they are paid the most
Future mergers will be agreed in secret, and staff will be told who goes only after the merger is complete
Future mergers will avoid cutting any jobs, whatever the duplication, so that the merged firm keeps two offices doing the same work
items.explanation: Publishing the duplicated roles, the method and the voluntary terms before signing removes the surprise and the age-based choice that caused the dispute. Cutting by recency or by age without discussion repeats the original choice, and agreeing in secret repeats the process that left staff with no say.

A rival offering a free tier is competitive pressure but not proof. The support team being small is a cost to manage, not evidence of conversion. Investors wanting growth and users asking for a trial are wishes, not evidence that the trial works.
options: Free users who are given a 30-day trial of premium features convert to paying customers at a rate of 25 percent
A rival firm offers a free tier with most features included

items.passage: A software firm sells a project management tool to small businesses. The tool has a free version with basic features and a premium version at 1,000 rupees a month with advanced reporting, integrations and priority support. Only 3 percent of free users upgrade to premium, and growth has stalled. The product head wants to make the premium features free for 30 days for all free users, arguing that users who try the features will see their value and pay. The finance head warns that giving premium features away will teach users to expect them for free, that support costs will rise, and that the 3 percent who currently pay may cancel and wait for the next free trial. The sales head suggests instead cutting the premium price by half, arguing that price is the barrier. The chief executive must decide before the next product release in six weeks, because the release locks the pricing page for the quarter and the firm has only enough cash for one major pricing change this year. The firm has 40,000 free users and 1,200 paying customers, and its cash will last for eight months at the current rate of spending. The support team has six people and already handles 200 tickets a day, mostly from free users asking for help with basic features. The sales head has argued that a price cut would bring in more paying customers quickly, while the finance head has warned that the firm cannot afford two pricing changes in one year. The product release in six weeks will lock the pricing page for the next quarter.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support offering the 30-day free trial of premium features?

Six weeks later, the product release has locked the pricing page for the quarter, and the firm has only enough cash for one major pricing change this year. The support team has six people and already handles 200 tickets a day. Five facts have come to light. (A) Only 3 percent of free users upgrade to premium, and growth has stalled. (B) Giving premium features away for 30 days will teach users to expect them for free, and the 3 percent who currently pay may cancel and wait for the next free trial. (C) The support team has six people and already handles 200 tickets a day, mostly from free users asking for help with basic features. (D) Cutting the premium price by half would bring in more paying customers quickly. (E) The firm has 40,000 free users and 1,200 paying customers, and its cash will last for eight months. Which combination of three facts MOST helps the chief executive reject the free trial for all free users?
options: (A), (C) and (D)
(B), (C) and (D)
(A), (B) and (E)
(C), (D) and (E)
(A), (B) and (C)
items.explanation: Rejecting the trial is justified by three legs: the upgrade rate is already low, so a trial must convert far better than 3 percent to help (A); the trial teaches users to expect premium features for free and risks the existing payers (B); and the support team of six cannot absorb a surge of trial users asking for help (C). (D) argues for a price cut, a different remedy, and (E) is about the firm's cash, which constrains every option alike. Every distractor triple contains two right facts and one that does not support rejecting the trial.

items.question: The firm has rejected the free trial and has cut the premium price instead. The finance head now asks for a rule that will stop the firm from ever again betting its cash on a single pricing change. Which rule best prevents a recurrence?
options: Premium features will be given free to all users for 30 days every quarter, so that users learn to expect them
The premium price will be cut by half every year, whatever the firm's cash position
The support team will be kept at six people, whatever the number of users, to save money
No pricing change will be made without a trial on a small group of users first, with the support cost and the effect on existing payers measured before the change is offered to all 40,000 free users
Pricing changes will be decided by the product head alone, without the finance head or the support team
items.explanation: A small-group trial with measured support cost and measured effect on payers attacks both causes: an untested change offered to everyone at once, and a decision made without knowing its cost. Giving features free every quarter repeats the expectation problem, and deciding alone repeats the process failure.

items.question: A retailer buys two mixers for Rs 1500 each, marks each 80% above the cost price, sells the first after a discount of 30% on the marked price and the second after a discount of 40% on the marked price. What is his overall profit percentage on the two mixers together?
items.explanation: Each mixer is marked at Rs 1500 x 1.80 = Rs 2700. The first sells at Rs 2700 x 0.70 = Rs 1890, a profit of Rs 390. The second sells at Rs 2700 x 0.60 = Rs 1620, a profit of Rs 120. The total profit is Rs 510 on a total cost of Rs 3000, which is 17%. The 26% option is the profit on the first mixer alone, and the others come from applying a discount to the cost price.

items.question: A boat travels downstream at 24 km/h and upstream at 16 km/h in a river. The boat goes 48 km downstream and then returns to its starting point, halting for 30 minutes at the far end. How long does the whole trip take?
options: 5.5 hours
5 hours
6 hours
4.5 hours
6.5 hours
items.explanation: Going downstream, 48 km at 24 km/h takes 2 hours. Returning upstream, 48 km at 16 km/h takes 3 hours. Adding the 30 minute halt gives 2 plus 3 plus 0.5, which is 5.5 hours. The 5 hour option forgets the halt, and the 6 hour option uses the upstream speed for both legs.

items.question: 6 distinct positive integers have an average of 15, and no integer in the set exceeds 60. What is the maximum possible value of the largest integer in the set?
items.explanation: The sum of the 6 integers is 6 times 15, which is 90. To maximise the largest, the other 5 integers must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, namely 1 to 5, summing to 15. That alone would give a largest value of 75, but no integer may exceed 60, so the cap binds: the largest value that can actually occur with 5 distinct integers below the cap summing to 90 is 60, and any larger value would force the smaller integers to repeat or to exceed the cap.

items.question: 6 distinct positive integers have an average of 18, and no integer in the set exceeds 95. What is the maximum possible value of the largest integer in the set?
items.explanation: The sum of the 6 integers is 6 times 18, which is 108. To maximise the largest, the other 5 integers must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, namely 1 to 5, summing to 15. That gives a largest value of 93, which is within the cap of 95, so the cap does not bind and the answer is 93.

items.question: Box P contains 4 red balls and 2 blue balls. Box Q contains 3 red balls and 5 blue balls. A ball is drawn at random from box P and moved, without being seen, into box Q. Then a ball is drawn at random from box Q and moved, without being seen, into box P. Finally, a ball is drawn at random from box P. Given that the ball finally drawn from box P is red, what is the probability that the first ball moved, from box P to box Q, was red?
items.explanation: Track the composition after each unseen move. If the first move is red, which has probability 4/6, box Q becomes 4 red and 5 blue. A red second move then has probability 4/9 and returns box P to 4 red and 2 blue, so the final draw is red with probability 2/3, giving a path probability of (2/3) x (4/9) x (2/3) = 16/81. A blue second move has probability 5/9 and leaves box P with 3 red and 3 blue, so the final draw is red with probability 1/2, giving (2/3) x (5/9) x (1/2) = 5/27. If the first move is blue, which has probability 2/6, box Q becomes 3 red and 6 blue. A red second move then has probability 3/9 and leaves box P with 5 red and 1 blue, so the final draw is red with probability 5/6, giving (1/3) x (1/3) x (5/6) = 5/54. A blue second move has probability 6/9 and returns box P to 4 red and 2 blue, so the final draw is red with probability 2/3, giving (1/3) x (2/3) x (2/3) = 4/27. The probability the final draw is red is 16/81 + 5/27 + 5/54 + 4/27 = 101/162. The probability that the first move is red and the final draw is red is 16/81 + 5/27 = 31/81. The required conditional probability is therefore (31/81) / (101/162) = 62/101. The distractors are the classic errors: 2/3 is the unconditional chance the first move was red, 101/162 is the probability the final draw is red rather than the conditional probability asked for, 31/81 is the joint probability without dividing by the probability of the final red draw, and 31/54 is the reverse conditional, the probability the final draw is red given the first move was red.

items.question: Two concentric circles have radii such that the inner circle has a circumference of 88 cm and the outer circle has a radius of 28 cm. A square is inscribed in the inner circle. What is the area of the ring between the circles plus the area of the square? (Use pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: The inner radius follows from the circumference: 2 times 22/7 times the radius is 88, so the inner radius is 14 cm. The ring area is 22/7 times (28 squared minus 14 squared), which is 1848 sq cm. The square inscribed in the inner circle has its diagonal equal to the diameter, 28 cm, so its area is 28 squared divided by 2, which is 392 sq cm. The total is 1848 plus 392, which is 2240 sq cm. The 1848 option is the ring alone, and the solver who subtracts the radii before squaring gets a planted wrong answer.

items.question: What is the maximum area of a rectangle that can be inscribed in a semicircle of radius 15 cm, with one side of the rectangle lying on the diameter of the semicircle?
items.explanation: Let the rectangle have half-width x and height h, with x squared plus h squared equal to 15 squared, since the top corners lie on the semicircle. Its area is 2 times x times h, which is largest when x equals h, that is when x is 15 divided by the square root of 2, giving an area of 225 sq cm. The solver who uses the full circle result, twice the radius squared, forgets that only half the circle is available, and the solver who takes the square of side 15 gets a smaller area.

items.question: By how much does the area of the largest square that can be inscribed in the full circle of radius 14 cm exceed the area of the largest square that can be inscribed in a semicircle of the same radius, with one side of the square lying on the diameter of the semicircle?
items.explanation: For the full circle, the largest inscribed square has its diagonal equal to the diameter, 28 cm, so its area is 28 squared divided by 2, which is 392 sq cm. For the semicircle, let the square have side s. Its two upper corners lie on the semicircle, so by Pythagoras s squared plus (s/2) squared equals 14 squared, giving s squared equal to 4 times 196 divided by 5, which is 156.8 sq cm. The difference is 392 minus 156.8, which is 235.2 sq cm. The 156.8 option is the semicircle square alone, and 392 is the full-circle square alone.

items.question: What is the sum of the areas of the largest square that can be inscribed in a semicircle of radius 11 cm, with one side of the square lying on the diameter of the semicircle, and the largest square that can be inscribed in the full circle of the same radius?
items.explanation: For the semicircle, let the square have side s. Its two upper corners lie on the semicircle, so by Pythagoras s squared plus (s/2) squared equals 11 squared, giving s squared equal to 4 times 121 divided by 5, which is 96.8 sq cm. For the full circle, the largest inscribed square has its diagonal equal to the diameter, 22 cm, so its area is 22 squared divided by 2, which is 242 sq cm. The sum is 96.8 plus 242, which is 338.8 sq cm. The 96.8 option is the semicircle square alone, and 242 is the full-circle square alone.

items.question: A cylinder has a base circumference of 88 cm and a height of 9 cm. A cone of the same base and height is hollowed out of it. What is the volume of the remaining solid? (Use pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: The base radius follows from the circumference: 2 times 22/7 times the radius is 88, so the radius is 14 cm. The cylinder's volume is 22/7 times 14 squared times 9, which is 5544 cubic cm. The cone removed has the same base and height, so its volume is a third of the cylinder's, 1848 cubic cm. The remaining solid is 5544 minus 1848, which is 3696 cubic cm. The 5544 option is the whole cylinder, and 1848 is the cone alone.

items.question: What is the remainder when 3 raised to the power 2027 plus 5 raised to the power 2027 is divided by 7?
items.explanation: Powers of 3 modulo 7 cycle as 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 with period 6, and 2027 leaves remainder 5 on division by 6, so 3 raised to 2027 leaves remainder 5. Powers of 5 modulo 7 cycle as 5, 4, 6, 2, 3, 1 with period 6, and 2027 leaves remainder 5 on division by 6, so 5 raised to 2027 leaves remainder 3. The sum leaves remainder 5 plus 3, which is 8, so the remainder is 1. The 5 option is the remainder of the first term alone.

items.question: What is the sum of all the EVEN positive divisors of 72?
items.explanation: From 72 equals 2 cubed times 3 squared, the sum of all its divisors is (1 plus 2 plus 4 plus 8) times (1 plus 3 plus 9), which is 15 times 13, which is 195. The odd divisors are 1, 3 and 9, summing to 13. Removing them leaves 195 minus 13, which is 182. The 195 option is the sum of all divisors, and the solver who adds only the even prime powers gets a planted wrong answer.

items.question: List all prime numbers below 30 as a1 < a2 < ... < an. For each i, let bi be the sum of all the primes in the list except ai, and let Xi = bi / ai. Let B be the set of all Xi that are integers. What is the smallest element of B?
items.explanation: The primes below 30 sum to 129, so bi is 129 minus ai and Xi is 129/ai minus 1. Xi is an integer only when ai divides 129, and among the primes below 30 only 3 divide 129, giving the integer values 42. The smallest of these is 42. The solver who computes all the values by hand, or who takes the largest prime, gets a planted wrong answer.

items.question: What is the largest integer n such that n squared is less than 10000, n is divisible by 11, n is NOT divisible by 7, and n - 1 is divisible by 5?
items.explanation: The largest integer whose square is less than 10000 is 99. Counting down through the multiples of 11: 99 is not divisible by 7, but 99 minus 1 is 98, which is not divisible by 5. Next 88: 88 minus 1 is 87, which is not divisible by 5. Next 77 is divisible by 7, so it is excluded. Next 66: 66 minus 1 is 65, which is divisible by 5, and 66 is not divisible by 7, so 66 is the answer. The 99 option ignores the extra condition, and the solver who forgets the exclusion takes 77.

items.question: Two numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 8 and x squared + y squared = 40. What is x cubed + y cubed?
items.explanation: The product must be derived before the cubes can be found. From (x + y) squared = x squared + 2xy + y squared, 64 = 40 + 2xy, so xy = 12. Then x cubed + y cubed = (x + y) cubed - 3xy(x + y) = 512 - 3 x 12 x 8 = 512 - 288 = 224. Checking directly, x and y are 2 and 6, and 8 + 216 = 224. The 512 option cubes the sum and forgets the correction term.

items.question: What is the minimum value of (x - 1) squared + (x - 6) squared + (x - 11) squared, where x is an integer?
items.explanation: The sum is minimised near the mean of 1, 6 and 11, which is 6. At x equals 6 the value is 25 plus 0 plus 25, which is 50. At x equals 5 it is 16 plus 1 plus 36, which is 53, and at x equals 7 it is 36 plus 1 plus 16, which is 53, so 50 is the minimum. The solver who minimises only the first two squares, or who takes the value at the midpoint of the outer terms without checking, gets a planted wrong answer.

items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that at least one of the dice shows 5, what is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 10?
items.explanation: There are 11 outcomes in which at least one die shows 5: five with the first die 5, five with the second die 5, and one with both 5. Of these, the ones summing to 10 are (5, 5), which is 1 outcome. The probability is therefore 1 divided by 11. The solver who divides by 36, or who counts only the outcomes with exactly one 5, gets a planted wrong answer.

items.question: How many real values of x satisfy the equation square root of (x + 5) + square root of (x - 3) = 4?
items.explanation: The domain needs x + 5 at least 0 and x - 3 at least 0, so x is at least 3. The left hand side is strictly increasing in x, since both square roots increase with x, so the equation can have at most one solution. At x equals 3 the left hand side is the square root of 8, about 2.83, which is less than 4, and at x equals 4 it is 3 plus 1, which is exactly 4. So x equals 4 is the unique solution, and there is 1 real value. The solver who squares both sides without checking the domain, or who counts the algebraic candidates from squaring, gets a planted wrong answer.

items.question: Is y greater than 5? Statement I: y squared = 49. Statement II: y is a prime number greater than 3.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Either statement alone is sufficient.
Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives y equal to 7 or to minus 7, so y may or may not be greater than 5. Statement II alone gives y equal to 5, 7, 11 or any larger prime, so y may or may not be greater than 5. Together, y must be 7, since minus 7 is not prime, and 7 is greater than 5, so both statements together are sufficient and neither alone is.

items.question: Which of the following statements CANNOT be true, given the data?

If Punjab's Maize production doubled, Punjab's total would exceed Uttar Pradesh's total

The combined total of Punjab and Haryana is less than the combined total of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh
